claim: Higher education_num and longer hours_per_week are each positively associated with the probability of earning >50K, as indicated by the large group difference between education_num and income (E4) and the small positive monotonic correlation between education_num and hours_per_week (E10), suggesting that more educated individuals who work more hours are more likely to be in the high‑income group.

Both higher education_num and marital_status categories are associated with income, as shown by the large group difference between education_num and income (E4) and the medium categorical association between marital_status and income (E6), indicating that education level and marital situation jointly differentiate income groups.

Marital_status and relationship categories each show medium associations with income (E6, E5), suggesting that family status and personal relationship type together stratify the distribution of high versus low income.

Sex is associated with both relationship categories (E1) and occupation categories (E7), forming a triad of categorical associations that reflect gendered patterns in personal relationships and job types.

Occupation categories differ across levels of education_num (E8) and also across workclass categories (E9), indicating that both educational attainment and employment sector shape the occupational distribution.

Relationship categories vary by both sex (E1) and marital_status (E2), and sex also varies by marital_status (E3), revealing intertwined social role patterns across gender, marital condition, and personal relationship type.

Education_num shows a small group difference across age groups (E11) and a positive monotonic relationship with hours_per_week (E10), suggesting that older individuals tend to have slightly higher education levels, which in turn modestly increase weekly work hours.
Both marital_status (E3) and sex (E3) exhibit medium categorical associations with income, indicating that family status and gender jointly differentiate high‑ versus low‑income groups.

Hours_per_week is positively associated with education_num (E10), and education_num is linked to occupation categories (E8), implying that higher education leads to occupations that tend to work more hours per week.

Age shows a small group difference across education categories (E11) and education_num shows a large group difference with income (E4), together suggesting that older age may be linked to higher income partly through higher education levels.
Sex is associated with relationship categories (E1) and also with marital_status (E3), indicating gender differences in both personal relationships and marital conditions.
Relationship (E5) and marital_status (E2) each show medium associations with income, suggesting that both personal relationship type and marital condition jointly relate to income levels.
Education categories differ across age groups with a small effect size (E11), indicating modest age‑related variation in educational attainment.
Education_num is positively monotonic with hours_per_week (E10), though the correlation is small, indicating that higher education modestly corresponds to longer weekly work hours.
Workclass categories are moderately associated with occupation categories (E9), reflecting that employment sector influences job type.
